claims.text: In single-phase concentrated alloys, the degree of local chemical ordering governs yield strength and deformation behavior.
Short-range ordered chemical clusters pin dislocations.
Equiatomic CoFeNi is a near-ideal solid solution with a nearly random atomic distribution and low intrinsic chemical ordering.
An Al addition has strongly negative binary mixing enthalpy with the CoFeNi base constituents.
Adding Al to CoFeNi can induce localized chemical clustering.
An appropriate heat treatment can promote short-range chemical order.
Single-phase high-entropy alloys can contain localized pockets of nonrandom atomic distributions.
Chemically ordered clusters act as barriers to dislocation glide and increase the energy barrier for dislocation motion.
Increasing local chemical order should increase yield strength relative to a near-random solid solution.
Increasing local chemical order may reduce ductility because of dislocation pinning.
Equiatomic CoFeNi exhibits ordinary solid-solution strengthening without additional cluster-mediated dislocation pinning.
The ordering effect should be significant when measurable short-range order is induced without forming secondary phases.
At sufficiently high temperatures, thermal disordering should diminish the strength advantage associated with short-range order.
The comparison should use single-phase alloys with identical casting and thermal histories.
A statistically insignificant change in strength and deformation behavior despite a measured increase in chemical clustering would falsify the proposed strengthening hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require the compared alloys to have the same thermal history, but one proposed intervention is a dedicated heat treatment intended to change ordering. That branch necessarily requires a different thermal history unless an additional matched thermal control is defined.
